course/heroText: Every command you type runs on a **simulated computer** in your browser that behaves like real Git (its output and commit hashes match Git 2.53). A **live graph** draws your history as it grows, and a shared **hub** lets you work with a teammate: push, pull, pull requests and all. Nothing to install and nothing to break. Each module goes **Learn → Practice → Play → Test**.
game/stagemanager/pitch: Only the right changes go on stage. Get exactly what each mission asks for into commits: no stray files, no lost drafts, one story per commit.
game/branchrunner/pitch: A target commit graph appears. Branch, commit, switch and merge until your graph has the same shape, in as few commands as you can.
game/conflictdoctor/pitch: Merges arrive with conflicts. Read the markers, write exactly what each case calls for, and get every patient out of surgery: no markers left, merge committed.
game/pushpull/pitch: Sam is pushing all day. Get your commits onto the hub without ever losing Sam's, and end in sync, before the clock runs out.
g01/title: Repositories, the three areas and commits
g01/tagline: What Git is, how a folder becomes a repository, and how changes go from your files into history.
g01/concept/g01-repo/title: A repository is a folder with a history
g01/concept/g01-repo/card:
**Git** records the history of a folder: every saved version of every file, who saved it, when and why. You can look back at any version, see what changed, and undo mistakes.

A folder whose history Git keeps is a **repository** ("repo"). `git init` turns the current folder into one. It creates a hidden **`.git`** folder: that's where the whole history lives. Your own files stay exactly as they are.

- `git init` = start keeping history for this folder (once per project).
- `git status` = "what's going on here?" Run it all the time: it's always safe, and it tells you what to do next.

Delete the `.git` folder and the history is gone, but your files stay: it's just a normal folder again.
g01/concept/g01-repo/example/note: `ls -A` shows the hidden `.git` folder. The prompt now shows `(main)`: you're on the branch main, waiting for a first commit.
g01/concept/g01-repo/cheat/note: Make the current folder a repository; ask Git what's going on.
g01/concept/g01-repo/predict/question: The folder is empty. What does `git status` say right after `git init`?
g01/concept/g01-repo/predict/choices/0: It lists the .git folder as a new file
g01/concept/g01-repo/predict/choices/2: An error: there's nothing to track yet
g01/concept/g01-repo/predict/why: A new repository has no history yet ("No commits yet"), and the folder has no files, so there is nothing to commit. The `.git` folder itself is never tracked: it *is* the repository.
g01/concept/g01-areas/title: Three areas: working folder, staging area, repository
g01/concept/g01-areas/card:
Your work moves through **three areas**:

1. **Working folder**: your files as they are right now. You edit them with any editor.
2. **Staging area** (also called the *index*): the draft of your **next commit**. You choose what goes in.
3. **Repository**: the saved history. Each **commit** is a snapshot of the staging area.

`git add FILE` copies a file's current content into the staging area. `git status` shows each file's state:

- **Untracked**: a new file Git has never been told about.
- **Changes to be committed**: staged, ready for the next commit.
- **Changes not staged for commit**: edited since you last staged it.

Staging lets you commit some changes and leave others for later: a commit should be **one logical change**.
g01/concept/g01-areas/example/note: Watch the 📋 Areas panel: `git add` moves the file into the staging area.
g01/concept/g01-areas/cheat/note: Stage one file; stage everything in the current folder (new and changed files).
g01/concept/g01-areas/predict/question: Two new files, but only `index.html` was added. What does `git status` show for `draft.txt`?
g01/concept/g01-areas/predict/why: `draft.txt` was never added, so Git lists it as untracked. `index.html` is staged ("Changes to be committed"), so it will be in the next commit; `draft.txt` won't.
g01/concept/g01-commit/card:
`git commit -m "message"` saves everything in the staging area as a new **commit**: a snapshot of the whole project at that moment.

- The **message** says *why*, in a few words: "Add home page", "Fix price typo". Write it as a command: "Add…", not "Added…".
- After a commit the staging area matches the commit, and `git status` says **working tree clean**.
- The first commit of a repository is the **root commit**: it has no parent.

Git prints a summary: the branch, a short **hash** (the commit's ID, like `d0469eb`), the message, and how many files and lines changed.
g01/concept/g01-commit/example/note: `git log` lists the history: here, one commit with its full hash, author, date and message.
g01/concept/g01-commit/cheat/note: Save the staged changes as a commit, with a message saying why.
g01/concept/g01-commit/predict/question: After the commit, what does `git status` report?
g01/concept/g01-commit/predict/choices/1: nothing to commit, working tree clean
g01/concept/g01-commit/predict/choices/3: Your branch is ahead by 1 commit
g01/concept/g01-commit/predict/why: The commit saved the staged snapshot. Your folder, the staging area and the last commit now all agree, so there's nothing to commit. "ahead by…" only appears when there's a remote to compare with.
g01/concept/g01-modify/title: Changing a file: modified, stage, commit
g01/concept/g01-modify/card:
Once a file is in a commit, Git **tracks** it. Edit it and `git status` shows **modified** under "Changes not staged for commit".

The cycle is always the same: **edit → `git add` → `git commit`**.

- A commit takes only what's **staged**. Edit a file, forget `git add`, and `git commit` says *no changes added to commit*.
- Shortcut: `git commit -a -m "…"` (or `-am`) stages every change to **tracked** files, then commits. New files still need `git add`.
- Changed it again after staging? Then it's in both lists: the staged version, plus newer changes not staged yet. `git add` it again.
g01/concept/g01-modify/example/note: `-am` stages the tracked change and commits it. `git log --oneline` shows one line per commit, newest first.
g01/concept/g01-modify/cheat/note: Stage all changes to tracked files and commit (new files still need git add).
g01/concept/g01-modify/predict/question: `index.html` was changed but not added. What does the commit do?
g01/concept/g01-modify/predict/choices/3: Asks whether to add the file
g01/concept/g01-modify/predict/why: Commits come from the staging area, which still matches the last commit. Git refuses and lists the modified file. Use `git add index.html` first, or `git commit -am "Welcome text"`.
g01/concept/g01-anatomy/title: What a commit is: hash, parent, author, message
g01/concept/g01-anatomy/example/note: `git show --stat` lists the files the latest commit changed.
g01/concept/g01-anatomy/cheat/note: The history, one line per commit; the latest commit and its changes.
g01/concept/g01-anatomy/predict/question: How many lines does `git log --oneline` print now?
g01/concept/g01-anatomy/predict/why: There are two commits: "Add home page" and, on top of it, "Add styles". The log starts at the newest commit and follows each parent back.
g01/concept/g01-identity/card:
Every commit records an **author**. On a new computer Git doesn't know you yet, and refuses to commit until you tell it:

```
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

`--global` saves it for every repository on this computer (in `~/.gitconfig`); you do it once. Without `--global` it applies to the current repository only, for example a work email for work projects.

`git config user.name` (with no value) shows the current setting. In this course's terminals your name is already set to **Alex Learner**, except where an exercise starts on a brand-new computer.
g01/concept/g01-identity/example/note: Now the commit works, and `git log` shows the author.
g01/concept/g01-identity/cheat/note: Once per computer, before your first commit.
g01/concept/g01-identity/predict/questio: This computer has never been told a name. What happens?
g01/concept/g01-identity/predict/choices: Git asks for your name interactively
The commit is saved without an author
g01/concept/g01-identity/predict/why: Git won't make a commit without an author name and email. It stops and prints the exact `git config --global` commands to run.
g01/item/g01-p1/prompt: Make a new repository in a folder called **`notes`** (inside your home folder, where the terminal starts).
g01/item/g01-p1/explanation: `git init notes` creates the folder and the `.git` folder inside it. `mkdir` alone makes a plain folder without any history.
g01/item/g01-p1/hints/0: `git init` can take a folder name; it creates the folder if needed.
g01/item/g01-p2/prompt: The repository `shop` has two new files. Stage **only `index.html`**: `draft.txt` must stay out of the next commit.
g01/item/g01-p2/explanation: `git add index.html` stages just that file. `git add .` would stage everything, including the draft.
g01/item/g01-p2/hints/0: Name the file you want to stage.
g01/item/g01-p3/prompt: `index.html` is staged. **Commit** it with the message **`Add home page`**.
g01/item/g01-p3/explanation: `git commit -m "Add home page"` saves the staged file as the first commit.
g01/item/g01-p3/hints/0: `git commit` with `-m` and the message in quotes.
g01/item/g01-p4/prompt: Save **both** new files in **one** commit (any message).
g01/item/g01-p4/explanation: Stage both (`git add .` or by name), then one `git commit`. Committing first does nothing: the staging area is empty.
g01/item/g01-p4/hints/1: `git add .` stages every new file in the folder.
g01/item/g01-p5/prompt: `index.html` was edited. Fill in the blanks to stage it and commit it with the message `Welcome text`.
g01/item/g01-p5/explanation: `git add` stages the change; `git commit -m "…"` saves it with a message.
g01/item/g01-p6/prompt: `index.html` was changed, but this commit doesn't save anything ("no changes added to commit"). **Fix it** so the change is committed.
g01/item/g01-p6/explanation: A commit only saves what's staged. `git add` first, or `git commit -am "Update title"`, which stages tracked files for you.
g01/item/g01-p6/hints/0: What does a commit take its content from?
g01/item/g01-p7/prompt: Read the status. If you run `git commit -m "Save"` now, what goes into the commit?
g01/item/g01-p7/explanation: Only staged changes are committed: `style.css` is under "Changes to be committed". The edit to `index.html` is "not staged", so it stays in your folder for a later commit.
g01/item/g01-p8/prompt: Put the steps in order: start a new project `blog`, write its first file, and save it in the history.
g01/item/g01-p8/explanation: Folder, repository, file, stage, commit. A commit before `git add` has nothing to save.
g01/item/g01-p8/hints/0: You can only commit after staging.
g01/item/g01-p8/hints/1: `git init` needs to run inside the folder.
g01/item/g01-p9/prompt: This is a brand-new computer: Git doesn't know your name yet. Set your name to **`Alex Learner`** and email to **`alex@example.com`** for every repository, then commit the staged note (any message).
g01/item/g01-p9/explanation: With a name and email set (once per computer, thanks to `--global`), the commit works.
g01/item/g01-p10/prompt: Show the history of `shop` with **one line per commit**.
g01/item/g01-p10/explanation: `git log --oneline` prints the short hash and message of each commit, newest first.
g01/item/g01-p10/hints/0: `git log` has an option for a compact view.
g01/item/g01-t1/prompt: Where does Git keep a repository's history?
g01/item/g01-t1/explanation: Everything Git knows about the repository lives in `.git`. `~/.gitconfig` only holds your settings, like your name.
g01/item/g01-t1/choices/0: In the hidden `.git` folder inside the project
g01/item/g01-t1/choices/1: In each file, as hidden lines
g01/item/g01-t1/choices/2: On the hub, never on your computer
g01/item/g01-t2/prompt: Commit **only `index.html`** (any message). `draft.txt` must stay uncommitted and unstaged.
g01/item/g01-t2/explanation: Stage just that file, then commit.
g01/item/g01-t3/explanation: It was edited and staged, then edited again. The staged version goes in the next commit; the newer edit is listed as not staged.
g01/item/g01-t4/prompt: `index.html` (already tracked) was changed. Commit the change in a **single command** (any message).
g01/item/g01-t4/explanation: `git commit -am` stages changes to tracked files and commits them in one go.
g01/item/g01-t5/explanation: Each commit points to the one before it; following parents from the newest commit gives the whole history. The very first commit has no parent.
g01/item/g01-t5/choices/0: the commit that came just before it
g01/item/g01-t5/choices/1: the folder it was made in
g01/item/g01-t6/prompt: Fill in the blank so the name is set for **every** repository on this computer.
g01/item/g01-t6/explanation: `--global` stores the setting for your user, so every repository uses it.
g02/tagline: Read the history, see exactly what changed, keep junk out, and undo mistakes safely.
g02/concept/g02-log/card:
`git log` lists the commits of your current branch, **newest first**: each with its hash, author, date and message.

Useful options:

- `--oneline`: one line per commit (short hash and message). The everyday view.
- `-3` (or `-n 3`): only the newest 3 commits.
- `--stat`: also list the files each commit changed.
- `--graph`: draw the lines between commits (it matters once there are branches, in module 3).

Labels in brackets show where things point: `(HEAD -> main)` means "you are here, on the branch main".
g02/concept/g02-log/example/note: `--stat -1` shows only the newest commit, with the files it changed.
g02/concept/g02-log/cheat/note: Compact history; the newest 3 commits; with the files each commit changed.
g02/concept/g02-log/predict/question: This repository has three commits. Which one is on the **first** line?
g02/concept/g02-log/predict/why: `git log` starts at the newest commit (where HEAD is) and follows each parent back, so the first commit ever made comes last.
g02/concept/g02-names/title: Naming commits: hashes, HEAD and HEAD~1
g02/concept/g02-names/example/note: `git show` alone shows HEAD with its changes: the green `+` line is what "Welcome text" added.
g02/concept/g02-names/cheat/note: The latest commit; the one before; any commit by its (short) hash.
g02/concept/g02-names/predict/question: The history is "Add home page" → "Add styles" → "Welcome text" (newest). Which commit does `git show HEAD~1` show?
g02/concept/g02-names/predict/choices/3: An error: HEAD~1 is not a commit
g02/concept/g02-names/predict/why: `HEAD` is "Welcome text"; `~1` goes one parent back, to "Add styles". That commit added `style.css`.
g02/concept/g02-diff/card:
`git diff` shows changes **line by line**: `-` lines were removed, `+` lines were added.

It compares different areas depending on how you ask:

- `git diff`: your **folder** vs the **staging area**: changes you haven't staged yet.
- `git diff --staged`: the **staging area** vs the **last commit**: what the next commit will contain.
- `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD`: between two commits.

So right after `git add`, plain `git diff` shows nothing: the change has moved to the staging area. Check `git diff --staged` before committing.
g02/concept/g02-diff/example/note: The same change, first as unstaged, then as staged.
g02/concept/g02-diff/cheat/note: Unstaged changes; staged changes; changes between two commits.
g02/concept/g02-diff/predict/question: You edited `index.html` and staged it. What does plain `git diff` print?
g02/concept/g02-diff/predict/choices/3: An error: the file is staged
g02/concept/g02-diff/predict/why:
Plain `git diff` compares your folder with the staging area, and they're the same now. `git diff --staged` would show the `+

Open daily

` line.
g02/concept/g02-ignore/card:
Some files don't belong in history: logs, build output, editor junk, and above all **secrets** (passwords, keys).

List them in a file called **`.gitignore`** at the top of the repository, one pattern per line:

```
*.log
build/
.env
```

- `*.log` = every file ending in `.log`; `build/` = the whole folder.
- Ignored files vanish from `git status`, and `git add .` skips them.
- Commit the `.gitignore` itself, so everyone on the team ignores the same files.
- It only affects **untracked** files: a file that's already committed stays tracked.
g02/concept/g02-ignore/cheat/note: Ignore every .log file; commit the .gitignore so the team shares it.
g02/concept/g02-ignore/predict/question: With `*.log` in `.gitignore`, which new files does `git status` list?
g02/concept/g02-ignore/predict/why: `debug.log` matches `*.log`, so Git ignores it. `.gitignore` itself is a new file like any other: it should be committed.
g02/concept/g02-restore/title: Undo changes you haven't committed: git restore
g02/concept/g02-restore/card:
`git status` tells you how to undo, and both use `git restore`:

- **`git restore FILE`**: throw away your changes to the file in your folder; it goes back to the staged (or last committed) version. ⚠️ Those changes are **gone for good**: they were never committed, so Git can't bring them back.
- **`git restore --staged FILE`**: take the file out of the staging area ("unstage"). Your changes stay in the folder, nothing is lost.

So: staged something by mistake? `--staged`. Made a mess of a file and want the last good version? Plain `restore`.
g02/concept/g02-restore/example/note: Unstage first (the change is still in the folder), then discard it; status ends clean.
g02/concept/g02-restore/cheat/note: Unstage (keeps your changes); discard your changes to the file (can't be undone).
g02/concept/g02-restore/predict/question: You overwrote `index.html` with "oops", then ran `git restore index.html`. What does the file contain?
g02/concept/g02-restore/predict/choices/: The last committed version (title and welcome line)
g02/concept/g02-restore/predict/why: `git restore` copies the staged version back into your folder, which (since nothing was staged) is the last commit's version. The "oops" edit is gone.
g02/concept/g02-revert/title: Undo a commit safely: git revert
g02/concept/g02-revert/card:
A bad commit is already in history. **`git revert COMMIT`** makes a **new commit** that does the exact opposite: lines it added are removed, lines it removed come back.

- The history stays honest: the mistake and its fix are both there. Nothing is rewritten.
- That makes it safe even after you've shared your commits with others (module 5).
- `git revert HEAD` undoes the latest commit; use a hash or `HEAD~2` for an older one. Its message is `Revert "…"`.

(There are commands that *erase* commits, such as `git reset`. They're for later: erasing shared history causes trouble for your team.)
g02/concept/g02-revert/example/note: The revert's diff is the bad commit's diff turned around.
g02/concept/g02-revert/cheat/note: A new commit undoing the latest commit, or any commit by hash.
g02/concept/g02-revert/predict/question: The latest commit, "Shorter title", introduced a typo. After `git revert HEAD`, how many commits does the log show?
g02/concept/g02-revert/predict/why: Revert never removes commits: it adds one more, `Revert "Shorter title"`, whose change puts the old title back.
g02/item/g02-p1/prompt: Show only the **2 newest** commits, **one line each**.
g02/item/g02-p1/hints/1: A number like `-2` limits how many commits are shown.
g02/item/g02-p2/prompt: Read the log. What was the **first** commit of this repository?
g02/item/g02-p2/explanation: The log is newest first, so the first commit ever made is on the last line.
g02/item/g02-p3/prompt: Show the commit **just before** the newest one (its details and changes), naming it relative to `HEAD`.
g02/item/g02-p3/explanation: `git show HEAD~1` shows "Add styles". `git show` alone shows HEAD.
g02/item/g02-p3/hints/0: `git show` takes the commit to show.
g02/item/g02-p4/prompt: `style.css` is staged and `index.html` has unstaged changes. Show **what the next commit will contain**.
g02/item/g02-p4/explanation: `git diff --staged` compares the staging area with the last commit: only `style.css` appears. Plain `git diff` shows the unstaged `index.html` change instead.
g02/item/g02-p4/hints/0: The next commit is made from the staging area.
g02/item/g02-p5/prompt: Your app writes `debug.log`. Create a `.gitignore` containing the line **`*.log`**, and commit it (any message). `debug.log` must not be committed.
g02/item/g02-p5/explanation: With `.gitignore` committed, `debug.log` (and every other `.log` file) stays out of `git status` and `git add .` for the whole team.
g02/item/g02-p6/prompt: You made a mess of `index.html` (not staged). **Throw away your changes**: put it back the way it was in the last commit.
g02/item/g02-p6/explanation: `git restore index.html` overwrites the file with the staged (here: committed) version. `--staged` only unstages, and nothing was staged.
g02/item/g02-p7/prompt: You staged `secrets.txt` by mistake. This command doesn't take it out of the next commit. **Fix it**: unstage the file, but keep it in the folder.
g02/item/g02-p7/explanation: `git restore --staged secrets.txt` unstages it; the file stays in your folder. (Then add it to `.gitignore`!)
g02/item/g02-p7/hints/0: Plain `restore` works on your folder, not on the staging area.
g02/item/g02-p8/prompt: The newest commit put a typo in the title. **Undo that commit** with a new commit, keeping the history.
g02/item/g02-p8/explanation: `git revert HEAD` adds `Revert "Shorter title"`, which brings the old title back.
g02/item/g02-p8/hints/0: There's a command that makes the opposite commit.
g02/item/g02-p8/hints/1: `git revert` and the commit to undo.
g02/item/g02-p9/prompt: Both files are staged, but only the `style.css` change is good. Put the steps in order: take `index.html` out of the staging area, commit `style.css`, then throw away the bad `index.html` change.
g02/item/g02-p9/explanation: Unstage before committing, or the commit takes both files. Discarding comes last (or after unstaging); it can't be undone.
g02/item/g02-p9/hints/0: A commit takes everything that's staged at that moment.
g02/item/g02-p10/prompt: Read the output. What did the commit before the newest one change?
g02/item/g02-p10/explanation: `git diff HEAD~2 HEAD~1` shows what changed from "Add home page" to "Add styles": a new file, `style.css`.
g02/item/g02-p10/choices/1: It added the welcome line to `index.html`
g02/item/g02-t1/prompt: Which command shows the changes that are **staged** (what the next commit will contain)?
g02/item/g02-t1/explanation: Plain `git diff` shows the unstaged changes; `--staged` compares the staging area with the last commit.
g02/item/g02-t2/prompt: Show the commit **two steps before** the newest one.
g02/item/g02-t2/explanation: `HEAD~2` is the grandparent of HEAD: "Add home page".
g02/item/g02-t3/prompt: `style.css` is staged, but it isn't ready. **Unstage** it, keeping your changes in the folder.
g02/item/g02-t3/explanation: `--staged` moves it out of the staging area only. Plain `git restore style.css` works on the folder instead, so the file would stay staged.
g02/item/g02-t4/prompt: The styles turned out to be a mistake. Undo the **"Add styles"** commit (not the newest one) without rewriting history.
g02/item/g02-t4/explanation: `git revert HEAD~1` (or its hash) makes a new commit that removes `style.css` again; "Welcome text" stays.
g02/item/g02-t5/prompt: The folder has `notes.txt` plus temporary files `a.tmp` and `b.tmp`. Fill in the pattern so **every** `.tmp` file is ignored, then everything else is committed.
g02/item/g02-t5/explanation: `*` matches any name, so `*.tmp` covers both files (and future ones).
g02/item/g02-t6/prompt: You edited a file for an hour (never staged or committed), then ran `git restore` on it by accident. Can Git give you the edits back?
g02/item/g02-t6/explanation: Git can only bring back what it stored. Edits that were never staged or committed are gone, which is why `git restore FILE` deserves a second look before you press Enter.
g02/item/g02-t6/choices/2: No: they were never in a commit or the staging area
g02/item/g02-t7/prompt: In what order does `git log` list commits?
g02/item/g02-t7/explanation: It starts at HEAD (the newest commit) and walks back through the parents.
g03/tagline: Work on several things at once without them getting in each other's way, then bring the work together.
g03/concept/g03-branch/title: A branch is a movable label
g03/concept/g03-branch/card:
A **branch** is just a **label pointing at a commit**. `main` is a branch too: it points at your newest commit, and moves forward each time you commit.

**HEAD** says which branch you're on: `HEAD -> main` in the log, a `*` in `git branch`.

- `git branch`: list the branches.
- `git branch NAME`: create a new label at the current commit. It does **not** move you onto it.

A branch costs nothing: no files are copied. That's why Git users make one for every feature or fix, and keep `main` working.
g03/concept/g03-branch/example/note: Both labels point at the same commit: the log shows `(HEAD -> main, menu)`.
g03/concept/g03-branch/cheat/note: List branches; create one (without switching to it).
g03/concept/g03-branch/predict/question: After `git branch menu`, which branch are you on?
g03/concept/g03-branch/predict/choices/0: menu: creating a branch moves you onto it
g03/concept/g03-branch/predict/choices/1: main: `git branch` only creates the label
g03/concept/g03-branch/predict/why: `git branch menu` creates the label (at the same commit as main) and stays where you are. `git branch` marks the current one with `*`.
g03/concept/g03-switch/card:
`git switch NAME` moves HEAD to another branch, and updates your files to match that branch's newest commit.

- `git switch -c NAME`: **c**reate a branch and switch to it, in one go (the usual way to start new work).
- New commits go on the branch you're on: that label moves forward, the others stay put.
- `git switch -` goes back to the previous branch.

Older tutorials use `git checkout NAME` and `git checkout -b NAME`: the same thing (`checkout` does other jobs too, which is why `switch` was added).

g03/concept/g03-ff/card:
**Merging** brings another branch's commits into the branch you're on: `git merge OTHER`.

Always: **switch to the branch that should receive the work** (usually `main`), then merge the other one in.

If your branch hasn't moved since the other one split off, there's nothing to combine: Git just slides your label forward to the other branch's commit. That's a **fast-forward**: no new commit is made.

g03/concept/g03-merge/title: Merging diverged branches: a merge commit
g03/concept/g03-merge/card:
When **both** branches have new commits since they split, Git can't just slide a label. It makes a **merge commit**: a commit with **two parents**, combining both sides.

- Git finds the commit where they split (the *merge base*) and combines both sets of changes.
- Different files, or different parts of a file: Git combines them by itself.
- The same lines changed on both sides: a **conflict**, which you resolve by hand (module 4).

The message defaults to `Merge branch 'about'`. `git log --oneline --graph` draws the two lines joining.

g03/concept/g03-merge/predict/why: The branches diverged, so a new commit joins them. They changed different files, so there's no conflict.
g03/concept/g03-delete/card:
Once a branch is merged, its label isn't needed: the commits are safely part of `main`.

- `git branch -d NAME`: delete a **merged** branch. Git refuses if it has commits that aren't merged anywhere, so you can't lose work by accident.
- `git branch -D NAME`: delete it **anyway** (for work you really want to throw away).
- You can't delete the branch you're on: switch away first.

Deleting a branch only removes the label. Commits that were merged stay in history.
g03/concept/g03-delete/cheat/note: Delete a merged branch; delete one even if unmerged.

g03/concept/g03-delete/predict/choices/3: Deletes the commit but keeps the label
g03/concept/g03-delete/predict/why: With `-d`, Git protects unmerged work and tells you to use `-D` if you're sure.
g03/concept/g03-dirty/card:
What happens to changes you haven't committed when you switch?

- If the other branch has the **same version** of those files, Git **carries your changes along**: they stay in your folder, uncommitted, and `switch` lists them (`M index.html`).
- If switching would **overwrite** them (the other branch has a different version of that file), Git **refuses**: *"Your local changes … would be overwritten by checkout"*.

Either way, nothing is lost. The fix is to commit first (or throw the changes away with `git restore`). A good habit: `git status` before you switch.

g04/tagline: When two branches change the same lines, Git asks you to decide. It's not an error, and nothing is lost.
g04/concept/g04-why/card:
Merging combines two sets of changes. Git compares each branch with the commit where they split:

- Changes to **different files**, or **different lines** of the same file: Git combines them by itself ("Auto-merging").
- The **same lines** changed differently on both sides: Git can't know which one you want. It **stops** and marks the spot: a **merge conflict**.

A conflict isn't a mistake or a broken repository. It's Git asking a question only you can answer. The merge waits, half done, until you decide.
g04/concept/g04-why/example/note: `title` changed line 1 and main changed line 3: different lines of the same file, so Git combines them by itself ("Auto-merging index.html"). Both changes are in the result.
g04/concept/g04-why/cheat/note: Both branches changed the same lines: you decide what the file should say.
g04/concept/g04-why/predict/question: main changed line 3 of `index.html` to "Open 10-4"; `hours` changed the same line to "Open 8-6". What does `git merge hours` do?
g04/concept/g04-why/predict/choices/0: Keeps main's version, because you're on main
g04/concept/g04-why/predict/choices/2: Stops with a conflict in index.html, for you to decide
g04/concept/g04-why/predict/why: Both sides changed the same line in different ways. Git won't guess: it reports `CONFLICT (content)` and waits for you.
g04/concept/g04-markers/card:
Git writes **both** versions into the file, between three marker lines:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version (the branch you're on)
=======
their version (the branch you're merging in)
>>>>>>> hours
```

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` starts **your** side: what the branch you're on has.
- `=======` separates the two sides.
- `>>>>>>> hours` ends **their** side, named after the branch being merged in.

Everything outside the markers merged fine. Only the part between them needs your decision.
g04/concept/g04-markers/example/note: `git diff` during a conflict shows both sides at once. Open ✏️ Files to see the markers in the editor.
g04/concept/g04-markers/predict/question: You're on main, merging `hours`. In `index.html`, which version comes right after `<<<<<<< HEAD`?
g04/concept/g04-markers/predict/choices/: main's version ("Open 10-4"): HEAD is the branch you're on
g04/concept/g04-markers/predict/why: HEAD is where you are: main. Its side comes first; the branch you're merging in comes after `=======`.
g04/concept/g04-resolve/card:
To resolve a conflict:

1. **Edit the file** so it says what it should: keep your side, their side, or a mix of both. **Delete the three marker lines.**
2. `git add FILE`: tells Git "this conflict is resolved".
3. `git commit`: finishes the merge. The message is ready (`Merge branch 'hours'`): `git commit -m "…"` or `git commit --no-edit` to keep it.

The result is an ordinary merge commit with two parents. Until you `git add` the file, Git refuses to commit, so you can't finish a merge with a conflict still in it.
g04/concept/g04-resolve/example/note: Here the edit keeps the longer hours (in the ✏️ Files tab you'd edit the file instead). After `git add`, status says "All conflicts fixed but you are still merging".
g04/concept/g04-resolve/cheat/note: Resolve, mark as resolved, finish the merge.
g04/concept/g04-resolve/predict/question: You fixed `index.html` in the editor, then ran `git commit` straight away. What happens?

g04/concept/g04-resolve/predict/why: Fixing the file isn't enough: `git add index.html` is how you tell Git it's resolved. Then commit.
g04/concept/g04-status/title: Where am I? git status during a merge
g04/concept/g04-status/card:
Several files can conflict in one merge. `git status` keeps track:

- **Unmerged paths … both modified**: files still to resolve.
- **Changes to be committed**: files resolved and added (and the ones that merged by themselves).
- *"All conflicts fixed but you are still merging"*: everything is added; `git commit` to finish.

Work through the files one at a time: fix, `git add`, check `git status`, next. The 📋 Areas tab shows the same thing.
g04/concept/g04-status/example/note: One file at a time; when status says "All conflicts fixed", commit.

g04/concept/g04-abort/card:
Not ready to decide? Merged the wrong branch? `git merge --abort` cancels the merge and puts everything back exactly as it was before you typed `git merge`.

- Your branch, your files and the staging area return to the state before the merge.
- The other branch isn't touched; you can merge it again later.

Only use it **during** a merge (when status says "You have unmerged paths"). Once the merge is committed, it's history: undo it with `git revert` instead.

g05/tagline: Share your repository through a hub: clone it, send your commits, bring in your teammate's.
g05/concept/g05-clone/card:
So far your repository lived only on your computer. A team shares one through a **hub**: a server that hosts repositories (GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket are real ones; ours is `hub.zilber.tech`).

`git clone URL` copies a hub repository to your computer:

- a new folder with the files, and **the whole history**;
- a **remote** named `origin`: Git's name for "the hub I cloned from". `git remote -v` shows its URL.

Your clone is a full repository: you commit locally, offline, as before. You only talk to the hub when you say so.

Your teammate **Sam** has a clone too. In the terminal, lines starting with `@sam` run on Sam's computer.
g05/concept/g05-clone/example/note: Sam's commit came along: a clone has the whole history. The 🌐 Hub tab shows the hub's copy.
g05/concept/g05-clone/cheat/note: Copy a hub repository; show where origin points.
g05/concept/g05-clone/predict/choices/1: The name of the remote: the hub URL you cloned from
g05/concept/g05-clone/predict/why: `git clone` records where it came from as the remote `origin`. Push and pull go there by default.
g05/concept/g05-push/card:
Committing saves to **your** repository only. To share commits, **push** them to the hub:

- `git push`: sends your branch's new commits to the same branch on `origin`.
- Afterwards `git status` says *"Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'"*.

A **new branch** doesn't exist on the hub yet. Its first push names the remote and branch, and `-u` remembers the link (the **upstream**), so a plain `git push` / `git pull` works from then on:

```
git push -u origin about
```
g05/concept/g05-push/example/note: Watch the 🌳 Graph: the commit flies to the hub's copy, and `origin/main` catches up with `main`.
g05/concept/g05-push/cheat/note: Send commits; first push of a new branch.
g05/concept/g05-push/predict/question: You committed `about.html`. Can Sam get it from the hub now?
g05/concept/g05-push/predict/choices/0: Yes: commits go to the hub automatically
g05/concept/g05-push/predict/choices/1: No: it's only in your repository until you `git push` ("ahead of origin/main by 1 commit")
g05/concept/g05-push/predict/choices/3: Yes, but only the file, not the commit
g05/concept/g05-push/predict/why: Commits are local. `git status` tells you how many aren't on the hub yet: "ahead … by 1 commit".
g05/concept/g05-tracking/title: origin/main: your last look at the hub
g05/concept/g05-tracking/example/note: After `git fetch`, the bookmark moves and status knows you're behind by 1.
g05/concept/g05-tracking/cheat/note: See remote-tracking branches; ahead/behind (as of your last fetch).
g05/concept/g05-tracking/predict/questio: Sam pushed a commit a minute ago. You haven't contacted the hub since cloning. What does `git status` say?
g05/concept/g05-tracking/predict/choices: "Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'"
g05/concept/g05-tracking/predict/why: `origin/main` is a bookmark from your last contact. Git doesn't check the hub on its own, so as far as it knows, you're up to date.
g05/concept/g05-fetch/card:
`git fetch` downloads the hub's new commits and moves the `origin/…` bookmarks. That's all:

- your own `main` doesn't move;
- your files don't change.

It's the safe way to look before you take: fetch, then `git log --oneline --all` (or the 🌳 Graph) shows what Sam did. When you're ready, `git merge origin/main` brings it into your branch.
g05/concept/g05-fetch/example/note: The banner only appears after the merge (a fast-forward here).
g05/concept/g05-fetch/cheat/note: Download the hub's commits; then bring them into your branch.
g05/concept/g05-fetch/predict/question: After `git fetch`, is Sam's sale banner in your `index.html`?
g05/concept/g05-fetch/predict/choices/1: No: fetch only downloads; your branch is now "behind by 1"
g05/concept/g05-fetch/predict/why: Fetch moved `origin/main`, not `main`. Status now knows you're behind; your files are unchanged.
g05/concept/g05-pull/card:
`git pull` does both steps at once: **fetch** the hub's commits, then **merge** them into your current branch.

- No new commits of your own: a **fast-forward**, your branch just moves up.
- New commits on both sides: a **merge commit** (the merge message names the hub URL).
- Both changed the same lines: a **conflict**, resolved exactly as in module 4 (edit, `git add`, `git commit`).

A good habit: **pull before you start working**, and before you push.
g05/concept/g05-pull/example/note: No local commits, so pull fast-forwards: Sam's banner arrives.
g05/concept/g05-pull/cheat/note: Fetch and merge the hub's changes into your branch.
g05/concept/g05-pull/predict/question: You made a commit (an about page) and Sam pushed one (a banner). What does `git pull` do?
g05/concept/g05-pull/predict/choices/1: A merge commit joining your commit and Sam's
g05/concept/g05-pull/predict/why: Both sides have a new commit, so the merge part of pull makes a merge commit (different files: no conflict).
g05/concept/g05-rejected/card:
If Sam pushed since your last pull, your push is **rejected**:

```
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
```

The hub won't accept a push that would throw away commits it has (Sam's). Nothing is broken. The fix:

1. `git pull`: bring Sam's commits in (resolve a conflict if there is one);
2. `git push` again.

g06/concept/g06-pr/card:
A **pull request** (PR) asks the team: *"please merge my branch into main"*. On the hub it shows the commits, the changes (a diff) and a conversation, where teammates review before anything reaches `main`.

Open one in the 🌐 Hub tab, or from the terminal with `gh`, the hub's command-line tool (the same commands as GitHub's `gh`):

```
gh pr create --title "Add footer" --body "A footer for the home page"
```

`gh pr list` lists open PRs, `gh pr view 1` shows one, `gh pr diff 1` shows its changes. A PR is about a **branch**: push more commits to the branch and the PR updates by itself.

g06/concept/g06-review/card:
Teammates **review** a PR: they read the diff and either **approve** it or **request changes** with a comment.

When changes are requested, you don't open a new PR. You just:

1. make the change on the **same branch**,
2. commit,
3. `git push`.

The PR picks up the new commit by itself, and the reviewer looks again. Reviewing each other's code catches bugs early and spreads knowledge through the team. (You can't approve your own PR.)

g06/concept/g06-merge/title: Merging the PR, then cleaning up
g06/concept/g06-merge/card:
Once a PR is approved, merge it on the hub: the **Merge** button in the 🌐 Hub tab, or

```
gh pr merge 1 --merge
```

The hub makes a merge commit on its `main` ("Merge pull request #1 from …"). Your computer doesn't know yet. Clean up:

1. `git switch main`
2. `git pull`: get the merge;
3. `git branch -d footer`: the branch is merged, its label isn't needed.

`gh pr merge 1 --merge --delete-branch` does all of that for you, and deletes the branch on the hub too.

g06/concept/g06-merge/predict/why: The merge happened on the hub. Your main is untouched until you switch to it and pull (origin/main isn't even updated until you fetch).
g06/concept/g06-protected/card:
Most teams **protect** `main` on the hub:

- no direct pushes: every change goes through a pull request;
- often a required **approval** from someone else before merging.

Pushing commits on `main` gets refused:

```
 ! [remote rejected] main -> main (protected branch hook declined)
```

That's not an error to work around; it's the rule. Put the work on a branch, push the branch, open a PR. (Our team's `main` is protected, with one approval required.)
